title: From Context to Contextualizing Processes: New Directions for the Study of Human Development
abstract: Abstract This special issue advances a dynamic reconceptualization of context in developmental science. Although contemporary developmental theories widely acknowledge that human development is contextualized, context has often been treated as an external and relatively stable set of conditions that influence development. In contrast, the contributions to this issue conceptualize contexts as an emergent, relational, and continuously evolving processes that both are shaped by and shape human action. Across six target articles, authors examine how individuals actively participate in the co-construction of bio-socio-cultural contexts through interaction, meaning-making, interpretation, imagination, and the use of symbolic and material resources. The articles further explore how different levels of analysis, from interpersonal and institutional to cultural and historical, are theorized and studied within process-oriented accounts of development. This issue also explicitly considers the implications of a dynamic view of these processes for research, practice and policy making. In the concluding article, the guest editors offer a Contextualizing Processes Framework around three themes: constitutive relationality, semiotic and material mediation, and the role of histories and futures in development and then state their hope that this Contextualizing Processes Framework can help research, practice, and policy to meet some of the challenges faced in a rapidly changing world.
